title: Dan Morgan pre-draft press conference | Carolina Panthers
text: All right. Uh, good to see everyone. Um, before we get, you know, to questions, uh, just want to take a moment to recognize, uh, all the people that are involved in the draft process. Uh, our scouts, our football ops, medical, uh, the coaching staff. Uh, there's a lot of hard work and dedication um, that goes into this. a lot of time away from families. Um, so I just want to recognize that and tell everybody, you know, thanks for that. Uh, we got a great team. Um, we're really excited about where we're headed, uh, with the draft. Um, we're nine days away now. Um, I really like where our where our board's at right now. I think we're in a good good spot right now. I think we're going to be ready. I know we're going to be ready for all scenarios that may present themselves at pick 19. Um, a lot of good players in this draft, a lot of guys that we like and that we're excited about. So, uh, it's going to be fun and and we're looking forward to that. Uh, I just want to mention, uh, we're looking forward to, you know, the fans being out there. We're having a walk outside with our first rounder the day after the draft. Um, so that'll that'll be a lot of fun. Uh, look forward to seeing a lot of the fans out there uh to greet to greet our first round pick. Um, you know, I know that obviously he'll appreciate it and I think uh the fans coming out here and and people greeting him. I I think it's going to be uh a lot of fun and and we'll definitely appreciate it and and I know the organization that will definitely appreciate it. So, uh, also beyond the draft, we're excited, you know, to get our guys back in the building under one roof. Uh, we start the offseason program. Uh, so we're excited about getting the guys back in the building. I know a lot of the guys already been in here working out. Uh, guys look great. A lot of guys offsite right now working out. Guys are working their butts off. There's a lot of excitement around the building. Um, we're certainly excited where we're headed. the direction that we're headed as a franchise and as an organization. So, uh, with that, I'll open it up to any questions. >> Dan, how different of of an exercise is this for you guys from where you were picking at eight and then when you were picking at 33 entering uh, day one of the draft the last two years? >> Yeah, I mean, I think it's a little different picking, you know, on the back half of the of the first round. Um, but it's really no different in terms of the process. I mean, we're going to be ready for any and all scenarios that present themselves. Uh, you don't know what gu is going to fall. Um, you know, a lot of things can happen on unexpected. So, we just got to be ready for any and all scenarios and and that's what we've been doing in the draft room every single day is just planning for that and and getting ready. I know we've asked you a lot about NIL and its impact on the draft, but how much do you weigh the age and potential second contract situation with the first round pick as well as injuries to especially notable ones entering Thursday? >> Yeah. Um, you I think you definitely have to weigh it. I think it's definitely part of the evaluation process. Um, but I also don't think it's everything and it doesn't, you know, take a guy out of the running because maybe he's 25, 26 years old. So, um, yeah, it's definitely something that we, you know, weigh in. Um, but it's it's not everything. >> In January, you said you guys were going to pick up Bryce's fifth year. Will you wait and do that after the draft or what's the timeline for that? >> Yeah. Yeah, we'll uh once the draft's over, we'll we'll definitely get that going. >> You guys have kind of done that the last few years, Icky, JC. If you know you're going to do it, why wait? Just from like the standpoint of, hey, you've made a decision already. >> Well, you know, I think uh obviously the player's not in the building yet, so you know, once once Brace gets in the building and uh you know, we're busy with the draft. It's off seasonason, you know, so we'll get that done as soon as he gets back in the building. >> Dan, the other week at the owners meetings, Dave said something about at 19, he doesn't think you can necessarily draft for depth. What does that mean to you? >> Um, you know, I I think, you know, I understand what coach is saying in terms of obviously you want your first round pick to be able to come in and contribute immediately. Um, so yeah, I'm kind of with him on that. uh you you want your first round pick to play, but you know there's different scenarios to where you know maybe it takes a guy a little longer to develop um and he may you know may not contribute right away but um you know with some of the picks at different positions you know it may take you know a little longer for those guys to develop for sure. what you guys did in free agency. Did that do you think that narrowed your focus positionally for 19 or does it >> No, I think if anything I think it opens opens us up to a lot of possibilities at pick 19. Um, you know, I think all positions are on the table and like I said before like you never know who's going to fall fall down to us. So, uh, I think we're definitely in the best player available mindset. Um, so yeah, I think what we did in free agency definitely set us up to do that. Dan, obviously with uh your decision to eventually pick up Bryce Young's uh fifth year option, um this is an really important year for Bryce and for this offense. How um much of a priority is it to get an extra playmaker on offense for him specifically? >> Um you know, I think uh you know, every year is important for everybody, including myself. Uh we we want to win. We're all committed to winning. Um you know, I think you know, Bryce is no different. you know, myself is no different. You know, we all are committed to winning. We all want to win. That's the ultimate goal is to win a Super Bowl. Um bring a championship back here to to Charlotte. Um you know, in terms of playmakers, yeah, of course, we always want to add as many playmakers as you can on both sides of the ball, not just, you know, a receiver. So, um, I think, you know, when we talk about the type of guys that we want to bring in here, we want guys that make plays. You know, whether it's a DB taking the ball away or it's a receiver, running back scoring touchdowns, we want guys that are going to come in here and be playmakers. >> I've heard you and Dave reference really wanting to know more about a player's story in addition to all of the facts and figures and stats. When did you adopt that as a priority in this process? Um, you know, I think uh I think really us getting to know guys. Um, you know, myself, Coach Canales, Brandt, our scouting staff, like when we're talking through guys, you know, I I feel like if you're going to miss on a guy, you're going to miss because you don't know the guy. You don't know what he's about from a personal character standpoint, and you don't know what he's about from a football standpoint. So, we want to find out as much as we can about these guys as possible. Um, understand how passionate they are about the game. Uh, what they do, what they like to do away from the game, like where are they spending their time away from the facility. Um, so I think all aspects of the player, we just want to know, get as much information as possible. >> To follow up on that, the the kind of the why of each player, how important is that when you're scouting quarterbacks? I know you brought up wanting to have a developmental quarterback in in scouting these guys during the process. How is how important is it to understand what makes them tick and how they can do that backup or third string job for a couple? >> Yeah, I think you know when you're when you're a backup or, you know, even like a third string guy, I think those type of guys that you want to bring in are guys that are going to support Bryce and and guys that also are competitors and they want to try to take Bryce's job, you know, per se. So we we want guys that are very supportive as teammates, but we also want guys, you know, that are going to come in and and they want to compete and they want to be great. >> When we talked to Brent, he talked about the three phases of building a team. I think he said building, contending, sustaining. Said he felt like you guys are in between building and contending. How do you quantify that? And then how as you approach the draft, how do you um look to move from building to um contending? >> I mean, I think, you know, our goal every year is to be a contender. Um that's the ultimate goal. Uh we're all here because we want to win. We all want to win. We're passionate about this team and this organization. Um, so in terms of the building part, like yeah, we're building a team. We're putting a team together, but the ultimate goal is for us to all compete um at a high level, everybody to give their best every single day, and that's towards the ultimate goal, which is to win a championship. >> Would you say you guys are still in the building phase or would you agree with his assessment? I would say we're in the phase to where we're continuing to add good players and and competing. You know, I think we have a locker room full of competitive guys that are hungry to win. We're hungry to win upstairs, downstairs, around the building. Um, so yeah, I'm definitely not going to box us into we're building this thing. Yeah, we're always going to be building this thing, but make make no mistake like we're we're in the mindset of going out there competing and competing to not just compete, but to win championships. >> Dan, we've seen Joe Gilbert at a lot of the offensive tackle pro days. Yeah. >> Some of the big names. How how big a priority is that position specifically at 19? >> Yeah. Um, you know, we we send position coaches, not just Joe Gilbert, to different pro days. So, it's not like, hey, we're just going to see all these offensive linemen. We're taking an offensive lineman at 19 or 51. Um, so yeah, I think the big thing is to, again, going back to what I said to Mike earlier, we want to get to know these guys as much as possible. So, as much exposure as we can have um you know with you know whether it's a tackle, whether it's a edge rusher, a linebacker, like we want to get close to these guys. We want to get to know them not only as players but but as people as well. >> And it feels like every year each draft kind of takes on a different personality like whether it's a quarterback year, pass rush year, old, young. just as you've gotten further and further into the evaluation, what is your biggest takeaway about this class? >> Um, you know, I think there's some guys in this class that we're really excited about and I think, you know, that goes from first round all the way down to sixth round. You know, we don't have a seventh rounder this year. Um, so, you know, I think it's our job to pinpoint exactly in those rounds who we have conviction on who was our type of guy that fits our scheme, but is also going to fit our culture, um, fit fit in our locker room and, you know, again, have that same type of passion that we that we've been talking about. >> Dan, you guys, uh, had to release Asan to open up cap space. He was a pretty big part of that defensive front. How do you feel about that group, but also how do you feel about the group in the draft at that like three tech, five tech? >> Yeah. Um, yeah, Asan, great dude, great leader. Um, we'll definitely miss him around here. Uh, it's definitely just part of the business. Um, but you know, in terms of the defensive tackle class, I feel pretty good about it. I think it's a little topheavy. Um, but I do think there's guys that we that we like that we've kind of pinpointed that we like. Um, so I think if the opportunity arises, we would definitely add competition and depth there. Um, you know, just like every other position. >> And kind of building off that, Brandt told us that y'all would have to make some room, the salary cap room. What's the timeline for those decisions? >> Um, th those are things that we talk through on a daily basis. you know, when we have to make the move, we'll we'll make the move. But, um, you know, there's different ways to to go about that and figure it it out. And, you know, luckily I Brandt Brandt's really good at that. And, you know, myself and him and Coach Canal is collaborating. You know, we'll figure a way. >> You've moved up and down the board in in both drafts. This is a draft where a lot of teams have multiple first round picks, multiple second round picks. Does that make it easier to have those draft trade conversations or does it make it so that maybe you kind of can figure out what other teams are doing from the standpoint of double dipping and and moving around? >> Um, you know, I I know we don't really look at it like that. Like we're, you know, even if a team has, you know, one second round pick, it doesn't matter. like we're we're always going to be watching our board, seeing guys fall off the board. And as they fall off the board, you know, if we feel like we need to make a move because maybe there's one person at a position that we really like that's left, then we'll make a move if we feel like we need to make a move at that time. >> Does the fact that you drafted a first round receiver two years in a row make it less likely that you would do that again? >> No, I think um you know, with anything, we're going to take the best player. So, if the best player we feel is that at 19, I wouldn't hesitate to draft another wide out. You know, I don't think there's a rule that says you can't draft a wide receiver three years in a row. So, I'm not really going to uh you know, I'm not going to box us in and and say we're not going to draft one. >> I think you've had several in the building. What do you think of that that group? >> I think it's a good group. Um, you know, I think receiver, you know, I think with all the seven on seven camps and kids growing up, like I feel like every year there's like wide outs that are super talented guys that are um, you know, you can tell they've been doing it a long time. So, I think it's another good class of wide outs and you know, I think you'll continue to see it that way. >> Tight ends. >> Yeah, I think tight ends, you know, I think there's a couple guys that are talented guys. Um, I do think, you know, there's some depth in the later rounds as well. So, um, again, if if they're the best player at a certain point, we wouldn't hesitate. >> Dan, uh, you've had a couple quarterbacks come on 30 visits this off season. Um, is that a product of evaluating them from a skill position perspective, from seeing if they're a cultural fit? Are you looking to draft a quarterback in the later rounds? Can you kind of just take me through your >> um Yeah, I think like bringing those guys in and bringing any guy that we bring in on a 30 visit, you know, it could be for medical, it can be because we just want to get to know them a little better. We want to see how smart they are, you know, if they can handle, you know, a big playbook, you know, and be able to retain it. Um so there's different reasons that we bring guys in for 30 visits. Um, you know, but usually it's just to, you know, get to know the guys better and and just figure them out a little more. >> Dan, going back to your tight end room, what are you looking for specifically in this draft to kind of mesh with those guys already in the room, but also offset the other weapons that you have on offense? >> Um, I feel good about our tight end room. Um, there's a a lot of guys in that room that are still developing. There's guys that have been here and we know who they are and and they bring a skill set that we really like. Um, again, like at every position, we're we're just looking for guys that fit, you know, what we do schematically. Um, you know, and fit with our culture. So, um I don't know that we're looking for any, you know, to answer your question, like any specific like skill set. You know, we're just looking for players at all positions that that can just make plays and really contribute to our team and our locker room. >> What's your outlook on the nickel position, big nickel or just your base set, but also the post position in your defense? >> Yeah. Um, you know, I think th those are areas that we've talked about and um, we do have some guys that we like that have played and and show they can play at that. Um, but again, I'm going to keep repeating myself like if you know the opportunity arises and there's a post safety that we like, then great, you know, we take a post safety. If there's a nickel that we really like and um, at a certain point, then yeah, we'll do that as well. So, I'm really, you know, myself and my staff and coach Canal, like we're all open to just drafting the best players that are on the board at the current moment. >> To follow up on that, I know the pick comes down to you, but there are premium positions and they're nonp premium positions. Do you feel like if there's a safety there or a tight end that falls and they are the best player on your board that you feel comfortable given, you know, the analytics department and all the value and all that stuff that you're willing to make a pick there? >> Yeah, I mean, those are all things that we talk through and, you know, we we discuss it and everybody has a voice in the room and everybody gives their opinions. Yes, ultimately I'm going to have to make the decision, but at the end of the day, um it's a collaborative effort. We're all talking through all these scenarios, all the value. Um those are all things we understand and you know, again, we wouldn't hesitate to to take a guy if we feel he's the best player. with where you are and, you know, heading into year three, do you think you'd be more inclined to to move back, collect picks, or go up for a guy? >> Um, I think we philosophically we have an open-minded mindset. So again, like we're open to anything, whether it's moving back, um whether it's moving up, you know, if we feel like a guy can be an impact player for us, I do think all options are on the table. >> Dan, when you talk about bringing guys in and getting to know him, what can a guy do during that visit to get your attention in a positive way? Um, you know, I think it's really the way again they're going to make a lot of contact around the building, whether it's with our strength and conditioning, our medical staff, um, our coaches, our the personnel staff. Like, there's going to be a lot of people that are going to interact with them during the day. Um, we usually get together afterwards and talk talk that through and, hey, what did you think of the guy? What' you think of that guy? uh we go around and get their opinions and you know maybe they act one way with me but you know with the trainer or something they're you know not as not as good of a guy. So yeah I think it's really just to bring the guys in and like get to know them a little more but not just me not just coach Canalis but like is he going to be a fit in our building >> is the biggest thing. Couple more. >> Go back to tight end. If how much has Bryce you think missed having that big target um in the middle of the field especially as far as able to expand what he can do? >> Yeah. You know, I think we have some guys on our roster that are that are big targets. Um you know, I think in general, you know, we have guys in our tight end room that that we feel are good players and and guys that have the skill set to be able to do that. And you know, I think opportunity, whether it's opportunity or whether guys are still developing, um, you know, I think we we have the pieces in that room to be able to do that. >> Do you know which players will not be available for OTAAS? >> Uh, no, don't really know that yet. Um, still working through. I think obviously Icky, you know, won't be available. Um, but I think pretty much the rest of the roster I think is looking in pretty good shape for that. >> JT, >> yeah, JT is doing great. Uh, he's running running, cutting, looking good. So, um, optimistic. >> You said you started with 600. How many names are you down to now? >> Oh, I'm not going to I'm not going to give you that number. It's easier to give the big number, but I'm not going to give you where we're at right now. But it's in a good spot. Anything else? >> Thanks, man. >> Yep. >> Thanks, guys.

title: What to Expect From Ravens' Pre-Draft Press Conference | Baltimore Ravens Final Drive
text: The NFL Draft is just over a week away and Wednesday we will get a sneak peek at how the Ravens brass view this draft class. General Manager Eric DeCosta and Jesse Minter will address the media to preview their strategy. Starting with pick number 14, DeCosta will have 11 picks at his disposal barring any trades. Now often called the liars luncheon by media as DeCosta plays his cards close to his vest [music] a week out from the draft lest another team get wind of who the Ravens favor. It will be DeCosta's first draft building a roster for new head coach Jesse Minter. But DeCosta said at the combine he doesn't anticipate that changing who the Ravens draft as they stick to their best player available mantra. Minter will be building his own version of the Ravens defense and talked at the combine about how he evaluates talent especially at the pass rush position. Number one production and I think there's a size speed length element we're kind of a requirement. Uh there may be guys that maybe are an inch or two shorter but then they bring something else really above the level um and so there's a there's a really wide variety of guys this year that have been really productive. Some that are third and fourth year, some that are fifth and sixth year the way the way college works now so uh I feel like there'll be a lot of guys in the draft that that could potentially help in that regard. Minter added that his collaboration will be very similar with DeCosta to the previous regime something he was familiar with in LA with the Chargers. The coaching staff will do deep dives on their respective positions and provide input. Wednesday DeCosta will share insight into what he believes the strength of this draft class are as his staff has dug into all the prospects. DeCosta made 11 picks last year as well and he values the influx of young talent that that brings as Minter's new staff will then be tasked to develop them. At last year's pre-draft presser he identified the 2025 class as one that had a chance to be really good for the Ravens also in the post-draft undrafted free agency phase. Something that proved to be very true when three undrafted rookies made that initial 53-man roster last August. So stay tuned for any gems like that in this week's presser but you may have to listen carefully to pick up on them. That press conference will be live-streamed on our Facebook page, YouTube channel, app and website Wednesday at 12:15 p.m. Thanks for watching. We'll be back with you tomorrow.

Um you know, obviously DeSean Jackson was a you know, if not a Hall of Famer, he's a really, really good player for a long time. >> with Alec is those guys were smaller. The Colts have to decide his future. You know, if you're going to play in the NFL, you need multiple corners. And buying them in Chidobe Awuzie Ward last year were pretty big swings in free agency. Um I want to get you out of here on this, Tom. The Carlie Irsay Gordon's been around these owners meetings, you know, for a a long time. Like when you talk to other people about Carlie, her name comes up. Her leadership or ownership comes up. What are those conversation What have kind of been the tenor of those conversations around the league with some of your colleagues just about the the new era of Colts ownership? Well, I think that, you know, I haven't spoken to a ton of people about it, but what I would say is um she's put in the time. And I think that that's the biggest thing that everybody wants. I mean, you know, the track record It's just like when she's making a decision at the end of the year of do you make major moves at head coach and GM or do you stick with Shane and Chris? Uh she stuck with him, but because there's no track record, nobody quite knew uh how she was going to operate. Um the fact that she stuck with them, I mean, it did reflect I think the patience that Jim uh had throughout his career. Um you know, I don't know Obviously, there's a lot of respect for Jim within the league. Um you know, but Carlie's her her own person. And so, we'll see, you know, as things move forward here. Yeah, last year was so unique. title: Exclusive interviews with Ron Brockington and Matt Winston | Miami Dolphins
text: What's up, Dolph fans? We are continuing our series here with Dolphin Scouts and Decision Makers, the folks that build the team here. I'm joined today by Brock Ron Brockington, senior national scout for your Miami Dolphins. Thanks for your time today, man. We appreciate it. >> Thanks for having me. I appreciate it. >> Yeah, we're excited to talk to you because a long journey across the NFL that brings you here to Miami, 20 years with the Dolphins, three decades across the NFL. We've been starting these off by just talking to you guys about your journey, man. Your path here. It's it's a long road to get to these spots in this league, and you've well earned it. I just kind of want to hear you talk a little bit about your your journey to the NFL and and where you are here today. >> Yeah, you know, I grew up in New York and um once I was done playing ball, I just I was still competitive. I wanted to find a different avenue that I still can be involved in and um you know, the NFL some aspect. You know, coaching was really not my thing. So, uh the next avenue was scouting and it's kind of how I got started. Uh I started my career at the Jets. Um Dick Haley was one of my mentors. um he really kind of got me involved in the business and what to look for and worked in a parcel. So um just a good group of of higherups to kind of show me and lead me the way of you know personnel evaluation. Um so that's kind of the path and then you know realistically I looked at it you know I had a proday and the numbers weren't weren't as good so kind of led to like obviously more like personnel stuff. So then uh kind of the rest is history. But you know you know that's a three decades is is pretty long. You know just consistency, discipline, just work ethic and just kind of staying in my lane has kind of been the the best avenue for me to be where I'm at right now. >> I love talking to former players that turn scouts because it does seem like coaching seems to be more of the avenue those guys funnel towards, but there's plenty of scouts that were ex players. Do you do you feel that that experience on the grass for so long gives you an advantage or kind of changes the way you see the game a little bit? I think it's a better lens um overall uh you know being in the locker room. So it's a little bit different. I just see in a little different lens. I'm probably at times a little bit harder especially when I'm grading running backs because I play the position. So that's that's a little hard for me sometimes just kind of separated but also know what really good ones look like. So >> right you're an expert in the field. So it's like you better be up to snuff otherwise I'm not interested in what you got going on there. But you also mentioned in that first answer a little bit about like going into coaching first then pivoting to scouting. That's also a common theme that I get from talking to people like yourself or coaches. they seem to kind of hit that fork in the road, then you make a choice. What was that for you that made you decide like scouting is the way for me, not coaching? >> Well, I I just fell in love with just the, you know, the why and and just building a team and and and again, Dick Heli was one of the best to do it. You know, you know, he worked with the Steelers in the 70s and he's built the steel curtain. So, you know, just being around him, it just opened my eyes to a different level and and that I didn't see in coaching. So, I just was intrigued by the personnel aspect and like I said, the why of how you build a team, how you build a steel curtain, you know, how do you win those championships and Super Bowls that that was, you know, my reason for wanting to go the personnel route? >> What does your time look like right now leading up to the draft? How what are you going through? How's your day-to-day, your schedule look like this time of year? >> Well, right now, we're kind of revisiting what we did in the spring, you know, post combine, um, pro days, um, you know, kind of revisiting some information, circling back. That's the thing you want to do now. security stuff, background stuff, medical, uh maybe calling some some sources back at schools or some of the guys we have targeted based on the February meetings. Um so that's what you want to do. Just circle back, make sure you know all boxes are checked um before the big day. Um so there's obviously you don't want any surprises. So that's kind of what's been the process. And then on the back end, just kind of just filling up, you know, the UDFAs, undrafted free agents, the back end, the roster. So that's kind of what we're working on this week. just kind of make sure all the stuff is is accounted for for you know so um you know Sully doesn't have to do any heavy lifting on on the back end. We've got all that completed for him. >> It kind of seems like the answer to this question is almost what you just talked about but the inverse of that in the fall when you're kind of getting going on the new class. How does that differ your day-to-day schedule now versus then where you are cultivating all that stuff you just talked about where you're kind of working from a big ball of clay now you've whittleled it down but how does it look when you're working with that initial you know fall scouting off the summer season? >> Yeah. Well fall is different. I mean that's kind of a foundation. Um you know where we start is Mark Island is our NFS pre meetings kind of get the the plan for where we're going. Especially for me is you know what big schools I have how I'm building out my schedule, what games I'm going to. Uh and then obviously dayto-day you know pretty much every day I'm in a different school and I kind of bleed that into the end of the week where sad I'm at a big game. So, it's a little bit of a different um schedule and and and work capacity compared to now where it's not as stressful because the travel is different. You know, I'm sitting here for a week as opposed to like everywhere I'm somewhere like Clemson, Georgia, South Carolina, like every day is somewhere different, you know, with a game on Saturday. So, no, not as stressful from a travel standpoint, but still the workload is is pretty similar. >> How many flights you take in a year, do you think? >> I'm you know what? Uh I get a lot of slack for this. I'm more of a drive guy. I I love to like get in my car. It's peaceful, man. >> Yeah, it's peaceful. I'm at my own pace. You know, I don't have to worry about, you know, missing a flight or delay. So, that's that's kind of me. You know, sometimes they look at me weird because I I'll drive long distance. For example, um just last week we're at I was at Nebraska's proday and I drove back to Indie. It's 9 hours and I started at 3:00. I got home at 1:00 a.m., you know, as opposed to flying. But again, I was at my own pace. I I was okay with it. You know, the last two hours were hard, but you know, again, I rather drive than fly. It's just me. >> I love the the the behind the scenes stuff from scouts, man. It's such a cool job because you guys are doing so much work behind the scenes that doesn't always get seen, but you know, talk about like an area scout versus being a senior national scout as your job has evolved over the years. What does that look like in terms of that, you know, you you have the scope of the entire country in a big job, all these schools, all these players. How do you balance going deep in terms of knowledge on players versus having a breath of knowledge of players across the country? Like do you do you have to differentiate like I'm going to focus on this amount of players or like this quality of players if that makes sense? >> Well, um I think it all starts from from being an area guy because that's the foundation of building relationships at different schools and that helps me um broaden out when I go to bigger schools or only have one stop, you know, because as a national scout, you can't circle back a lot of times because the volume of schools or the area is so big. So, you got to trust your relationships. You got to trust your work ethic, your ability to get it all done in one day, which is it's it's pretty hard. And, you know, there's times my week will be like Georgia, South Carolina, Clemson. That's a lot of evaluation. There's a lot of top end players. That's a lot of guys that, you know, are we will be considered for the draft. So, I mean, it's hard, but I got to rely on my contacts, um, the area guys, communicating with them to make sure the foundation is laid up, like who exactly am I looking at, you know, because I can't waste time. I gotta I gotta keep moving because again the volume of schools and I got to keep going on to the next because I don't have the advantage of circling back like the area guys. So um it's it's nothing that's you know again I'm a competitive guy. I like to challenge. I like to you know be in a situation where it's hard and it is hard but it's good. Again, you build relationships and there's a lot of coaches that's come through Miami or just over the course of my career that I've built relationships where I can call or circle back or, you know, I'm out at practice, I can pull it aside and they may, you know, steer me one way or another or at least give me another piece of information. So, it it helps to know people at the end of the day because it's a relationship business. >> Absolutely. It's a little different when you're going to a a blue blueb blood program that has maybe 10 five stars versus a directional school that has one guy, right? >> Yes. A lot easier. A lot easier. >> A lot different. So, something else I wanted to kind of close here with with you was you worked as a group leader at the NFL combine for multiple years in a row. Just kind of wanted to pick your brain on what that entails and what you enjoy about the process and maybe what you learned from that entire process. >> First of all, it it's unique and I love it. Like I'm I'm like I'm driven outside of Dolphins. That's like that's like my pet project. Um, you know, each year I'm excited about the list. I see the list when men sends me the combine list. Um, you know, I kind of go through it. First of all, this the hard part is the pronunciation of names. So, I go through this. I'm like, who's these hard names I got to pronunciate? Cuz I got to get on the mic and announce these guys. So, that's that's probably number one. But number two is, you know, I got four days to spend with these players. I mean, um, a lot of these guys, uh, I've seen or visited at the school, so I got a sense of who they are and what they are from a background standpoint. And, and you'd be shocked. A lot of these guys are completely different, good and bad. U, but just four days around somebody, you know, just lining up. Where's your name tag? you know, who's on time, who's late, who communicates, who has a good personality. I mean, I love it just being it's another checkpoint just being around the players and it helps us, you know, because, you know, we may be on a clock or come up in meetings like, well, this guy was in my group, you know, he was a good player, you know, good character, he's on time or the opposite, like, you know, this guy was always late, you know, had the wrong gear on. So, it's it's just another checkpoint to help us uh get to know the player. So, I mean, I love it. Yeah. And I've been doing it for multiple years. And and it's funny because um last night I ran into T Dot and uh JB and I was like I said, "It's a small role." And they was like, they kind of looked at me funny. I said, "You guys don't realize I was your group leader at the combine." And they kind of thought back and they kind of caught him off. Yeah. Oh yeah. So I mean it is a small role. Willie Gay, I mean those are players that I had under me in in um at the combine, you know, so it works out. >> Last one for you here. Uh so has described the process as collaboration with boundaries and trust. You've talked a lot about relationships already. How would you describe the collaboration with the rest of the department in this pre-draft process here in 26? >> Oh, it's I mean from you guys to trainers to Drew. I mean I mean it's it's it's all hands on deck. I mean at the end of the day I mean you know after a pro day the first thing I got to do is, you know, send out an email to to to Kyle and to for injuries or if anything pops up from a security standpoint to Drew and I got a CC Sully and Kyle. So, I mean, like it's it's a chain of emails and just communication to make sure we're all on the same page. Again, no surprises. So, uh again, it's a team effort. It's a team effort in all aspects. I mean, everybody's got to be on board. I mean, think about it. We're investing in our future. We all want to win. We all want a championship. So, we got to make sure the player we select, you know, fits the criteria to be a Miami Dolphin. So, I mean, it's it's a team effort. >> Yeah, absolutely. He's on the team that builds a team for the Miami Dolphins. Ron Brockington, senior national scout. Appreciate your time today, man. That was great. Thank you. >> Appreciate it. very special guest, the director of college scouting for your Miami Dolphins, Matt Winston. Matt, welcome back into the show, man. >> Thanks for having me. >> I'm excited to have you on here. How's things been for you? We haven't spoken since, I believe, last combine. >> Yeah. Yeah, it's busy. Busy obviously this time of year. >> So, during your time here at the Miami Dolphins, you've had responsibilities all across the board, pro and college. Can you kind of pull the curtain back on that a little bit? Explain the difference in terms of duties, responsibilities from college versus a pro scout. >> Yeah. Um, it's vastly different. um the the pro scouting side, you know, you're you're in the office basically, you know, 3 365. Um outside of some advanced work, travel or traveling with the team, you know, you're you're with the team dayto-day, you're much more in tune with what's going on. Um and then and then the pro scouts also handle the advance evaluations for for the for uh for our opponents. How many how many total players would you say that you like could rip off their like their report on a given like at a moment's notice? >> Oh, >> across the league, college, it seems like it's in the thousands. >> Quite a few. I mean, that's the thing after you've been doing this for so many years, you know, you just build your rolodex every year and it just compounds and compounds and so yeah, you get to you get to a pretty deep rolodex and then you you start to forget some some of them that you wrote a long time ago.
